name: crystalline CaTiO3 (an upper bound on its absorption)

licence: reduced values from Kitzmann and Heng 2018's compilation, the only machine-readable copy found, cited to the primary and to Kitzmann and Heng as the compiler: the measured values are the authors' facts, and the repository's GPL-3.0 covers its code and arrangement, not a reduced visible subset of one material; its compilation/readme.txt sets no separate terms for the data. No compilation file and none of LX-MIE's code is committed (decision-composition §5; decision-r08-licences.md)
reduction: n linear and k linear in log k in wavelength between the source's rows, onto 380–780 nm every 5 nm, to six significant figures; the source's rows are about 3.6–7.7 nm apart here. No open copy of Ueda et al.'s visible values was found. The copy states no temperature. Its visible k is not a measurement of absorption (R08.T5.i, decision-p14-t49c-split §5.3), and the file keeps it as an upper bound on the pure crystal's sub-gap k, a stated stand-in. Ueda et al.'s abstract: "Normal incidence light reflection measurements have been performed for single crystals over the wide energy region from 0.4 to 35 eV. The dielectric functions and optical constants are evaluated from the reflectance spectrum by the Kramers-Krönig transformation technique" (through OpenAlex, https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1088/0953-8984/10/16/018, SHA-256 30d02af069bb67a91cd07186919db44614faaa4c42db12bda711ff61f8523a3d, fetched 2026-10-16; the article is closed). At 550 nm, n 2.33245, the normal reflectance is 0.1598728 with k = 0 and 0.1598730 with the file's k of 1.81089 × 10⁻³, a change of 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ (computed): reflectance cannot see a k this small, so the measurement does not constrain the sub-gap k, which comes from the transform, as Kitzmann and Heng read it from Ueda et al.'s figure (their Table 1, "Data available as figure"; the arXiv copy, arXiv:1710.04946v2, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.04946v2, SHA-256 ba36c5a2cc6ee4dc71fbf11d461301324f1e144d3700d72f61d1ebb8e83723ec, fetched 2026-10-16). 380–780 nm is 3.26–1.59 eV, below the compiled crystal's absorption edge near 3.65 eV (its k is 0.027 at 3.62 eV and 0.058 at 3.67 eV, the compilation's rows) and below the band gap of 3.8–4.38 eV that Krause, Weber, Pohl, Rellinghaus, Kersch and Mikolajick 2015 measure in ultrathin layers by low-energy EELS (electron energy loss spectroscopy) ("Investigation of band gap and permittivity of the perovskite CaTiO3 in ultrathin layers", J. Phys. D 48, 415304, DOI 10.1088/0022-3727/48/41/415304; their abstract, through OpenAlex, https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1088/0022-3727/48/41/415304, SHA-256 23e4cb27986c8707e63d04a1f403ce90b9b6ab5440f9b41f52bad43bd2cb68e4, fetched 2026-10-16; the article is closed, so their DUV–VIS ellipsometry was not read). The Handbook of Mineralogy's perovskite sheet (J. W. Anthony, R. A. Bideaux, K. W. Bladh and M. C. Nichols, Mineral Data Publishing, version 1, https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/perovskite.pdf, SHA-256 c8f43952ab901561cf0a922bc47b17579ee2cdc9d80188ccf2c7d1065c6c62a6, fetched 2026-10-16) describes the natural mineral, whose Vogtsberg analysis there carries 25.99% Nb2O5, 5.69% FeO and 3.08% RE2O3, as "Opaque, transparent in thin fragments", "colorless to dark brown in transmitted light", with a "White to grayish white" streak and n = 2.34–2.37. At the file's k a 30 µm section, a standard thin section's thickness (Wikipedia, "Thin section", revision 1323745730, https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thin_section&oldid=1323745730, SHA-256 66633dded2f05cad0e37e0e2531a082b8dd19f7e90371e426289b5c4decd51b4, fetched 2026-10-16), would transmit 2.1% at 450 nm and 29% at 550 nm before reflection losses, absorption lengths of 7.8 and 24 µm (computed): a section colourless in transmitted light is not possible at these values, even of the impure mineral, so the file's k lies above the crystal's absorption, and a colourless crystal would draw brighter. The k is kept rather than set to 0, since no measurement says the absorption is nil, and a changed k would need the phase table remade; a transmission measurement, if one is found, replaces it. R08.T5.i's search (2026-10-16) found none that could be read: A. Linz and K. Herrington, "Electrical and Optical Properties of Synthetic Calcium Titanate Crystal", J. Chem. Phys. 28 (1958) 824–825, DOI 10.1063/1.1744278, whose abstract reads "The optical density of a flame fusion single crystal plate of CaTiO3 is reported. The refractive indices for the visible region are given, with nD = 2.403±0.02" (through Crossref, https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1063/1.1744278, SHA-256 da8e8cc24a8adf62dbaefcf9b302a5b12111e351d6c87872a298dd81ac5cf81c, fetched 2026-10-16); the article is closed and its values were not read, so it is the lead for that measurement
standIn: an upper bound on absorption, since it is drawn with a published visible k that is a Kramers–Kronig value from normal-incidence reflectance, which cannot detect a k this small, and thin sections of the mineral can be colourless, so the pure crystal absorbs less
